item.title: Kyoto Cooking Class Guide: Learn Japanese Home Cooking
item.description: A cooking class is one of the most rewarding things a food-loving visitor can do in Kyoto — and one of the few souvenirs you can take home and use forever. In a few hours, a friendly local instructor teaches you to make real Japanese home cooking — washoku staples, Kyoto’s vegetable-forward obanzai, sushi, ramen, or delicate wagashi sweets — often after a guided shop through Nishiki Market to choose your ingredients.

item.title: Nishiki Market Guide: Kyoto's Kitchen, Stall by Stall
item.description: For four centuries, “Kyoto’s Kitchen” has run down a single narrow, covered lane in the heart of downtown. Nishiki Market is 400 metres of more than a hundred stalls and shops selling everything that defines Kyoto cuisine: mountain vegetables, dozens of kinds of pickles, fresh tofu and yuba, sweets, knives, tea, dried seafood, and an ever-growing array of street snacks to eat as you go. It is the single best place to taste and understand the ingredients behind Kyoto’s refined food culture.

item.title: Kyoto Food Guide: Kaiseki, Obanzai, Matcha & Nishiki Market
item.description: Kyoto’s cuisine is the most refined in Japan — and the most misunderstood. Visitors arrive expecting expensive multi-course meals and leave having eaten mostly convenience store food, unsure where to find the real thing at a reasonable price. This guide explains the food culture properly: what kaiseki actually is, where the affordable versions are, what obanzai is, why Kyoto matcha is different, and where the locals eat. 懐石料理 — Kaiseki: Japan’s Highest Culinary Art Kaiseki (懐石料理) evolved from the simple meal served before a tea ceremony — a small gathering of seasonal vegetables, pickles, and rice intended to calm the stomach before consuming bitter matcha.
